graduation_requirements.raw_text:
Graduation Requirements

Graduation requirements for MUHS students are as follows:
Students must earn a minimum of 22.5 credits with the following distribution:

                Language and Literature                                     4 credits
                Language Acquisition                                      1 credit (2 recommended)
                Individuals and Societies                                   3 credits
                Sciences                                                   3 credits
                Mathematics                                                3 credits
                Arts/Design                                                 2 credits
                Physical Education                                         1.5 credits
                Health Education                                           1 credit
                Theory of Knowledge                                        0.5 credits
                Electives                                                  3.5 credits

Required Course Load
Students at MUHS are required to carry a minimum of seven academic credits per year in grades 9
through 11. Students in grade 12 are required to carry a minimum of 6 credits. Students are encouraged
to consider a challenging academic course load to be fully prepared for further education or the world of
work.

All of the above courses in the distribution are aligned with National and State Standards and assessed
based on four subject-specific criteria. Successful completion of these courses indicates proficiency (a
Criterion Level Total score of 15 or higher with no individual scores below 3). See the MUHS Teaching
and Learning Guide for more information.

In addition, students complete a Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) in grades 9 - 12 which includes the
Grade 10 Personal Project. This learning opportunity is scored on a pass/ fail basis and passing students
will earn 0.25 elective credits, and makes students eligible to enroll as full DP candidates at the beginning
of grade 11.

Those completing the full International Baccalaureate (IB) Diploma Program (DP) have specific
requirements further defining this distribution, including the completion of an Extended Essay and
Creativity, Activity, Service (CAS).

courses.course_name: Fundamentals of Language and Literature, MYP Year 4
courses.description: Students in this course study novels, plays, short stories, memoirs, rhetoric, and poetry. Basic composition skills, sentence structure, analytical paragraphs, essays, vocabulary, and usage are integrated with the texts. Literacy activities, organization techniques, and study skills are emphasized.
courses.fulfills_text: Each student must enroll in the 100-level course (MYP Year 4 Language & Literature) and the 200-level (MYP Year 5 Language & Literature) course during their first two years at MUHS.

courses.description: This course centers on the development of students’ writing strategies by continuing the work of MYP4. Students study graphic narratives, speeches, epistles, op-eds, plays, and novels to develop analytical and creative abilities both in reading and writing. Students build skills in analyzing, organizing, producing text, and using language.
courses.fulfills_text: Each student must enroll in the 100-level course (MYP Year 4 Language & Literature) and the 200-level (MYP Year 5 Language & Literature) course during their first two years at MUHS.

courses.description: This course promotes the ability to form independent literary judgments and develops an understanding of the techniques involved in literary criticism. Over the course, the formal analysis of texts and wide coverage of a variety of literature—both in the language of the subject and in translated texts from other cultural domains—is combined with a study of the way literary conventions shape responses to texts. Students completing this course will develop a thorough knowledge of a range of texts and an understanding of other cultural perspectives. They will also develop skills of analysis and the ability to support an argument in clearly expressed writing, sometimes at significant length.

This course will cover all of the topics covered in the Literature SL course, plus additional topics and required texts. The HL course moves faster and covers more content, and contains more DP assessments. The Higher Level Essay is completed in the spring of Year 1.

This course aims to develop skills of textual analysis of both literary and non-literary texts from a variety of sources, genres, and media. A key aim of this course is to encourage students to question the meaning generated by language and texts, which, it can be argued, is rarely straightforward.

This course covers all of the topics covered in the Language and Literature SL course and also includes additional topics and students will be required to read additional texts. The HL course moves faster, covers more content, and contains more DP assessments.

courses.course_name: Popular Fiction: Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror
courses.description: In this course, students will explore speculative fiction. Students will read a variety of short- and long-form fiction, including books of their own choosing, in three different genres. Literary conventions and social contexts will be explored through discussion, creative writing and formal analysis.

courses.course_name: Popular Fiction: Real Life, Then & Now
courses.description: In this course, students will explore realistic fiction, historical fiction, memoir and travelogues. Students will read a variety of texts that illustrate ordinary life and extraordinary circumstances, personal journeys, and the past. Literary conventions and genre terminology will be instructed, and students will produce reflective, narrative and analytical assessments.

This course examines the major themes of our nation’s earlier writers, and emphasizes analysis in discussion and writing. The course aim is to heighten the student’s awareness of the literature reflective of American culture prior to 1900. Students will read selected novels, poems, plays, stories, and essays from writers like Edgar Allen Poe, Henry David Thoreau and Walt Whitman.

This course examines the major themes of 20th and 21st century writers, and emphasizes analysis in discussion and writing. The course aim is to heighten the student’s awareness of the literature reflective of American culture after 1900. Students will read selected novels, poems, plays, stories, and essays from writers like F. Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway and Sylvia Plath.
This course builds on the aspects of Year 1 with special attention paid to the DP assessments: the Oral, Paper 1, and Paper 2. Prerequisite: Successful completion of DP Literature (SL or HL) Year 1.

courses.description: Creative Writing I is a workshop-based course for 11th- and 12th-grade students interested in exploring their own writing in a collaborative environment. Students focus on creative nonfiction, memoir, personal narrative, and short fiction, using peer and teacher conferences to support experimentation, free expression, and revision.The course incorporates a variety of media and models, including literary nonfiction, literary fiction, and selected graphic or digital narratives, to highlight different approaches to voice and structure. Throughout the semester, students complete a series of writing projects, participate in workshops, and maintain a learning portfolio of drafts and polished pieces that they share with their peers.

Creative Writing II is an independent, workshop-based course open to all 11th- and 12th-grade students, with no prerequisite. This course emphasizes poetry, drama and dialogue, and oral storytelling, while also inviting students to experiment with additional forms such as thriller elements, dramatic scenes, and graphic or hybrid narratives. Students engage in writing projects, readings, and performances that foreground image, rhythm, subtext, and pacing, using peer and teacher conferences to refine their work. As in Creative Writing I, students assemble a learning portfolio that documents multiple drafts and finished pieces across genres and are expected to share selected work with classmates through workshops, readings, or informal performances.

In Exploring Film Genres, students will delve into the world of film’s various cinematic aspects (such as cinematography, mise en scene, composition, and narrative structure), while simultaneously exploring how different genres of film (comedy, horror, noir, documentary, action, etc.) use these aspects in distinct ways. Students will “read” a wide variety of films from different genres, interpreting filmmaker choices and analyzing films’ meanings and qualities.

Critical Studies in Cinema gives students a great deal of practice in critically watching, reading about, and writing about film. By looking at film as a text to be studied and interpreted, students will consider elements such as setting and cinematography, narrative strategy and point of view, character development, dialogue, and pacing. Thematically, students will learn how to apply a different critical lens to film by studying theories such as race, gender, and class, among others. Additionally, students will be instructed on technical aspects (camera angle, blocking, mise en scene, focus, etc.) of film.

Mythology, history, culture and language are all explored in this beginning course designed as an introduction to the ancient Romans and their language. Emphasis is placed on acquiring the skills needed to read elementary Latin texts. The influence of Roman civilization on modern society is examined through a study of Roman mythology, culture, history, art, and archeology. Southern Italy and the city of Pompeii are heavily featured in geography. In addition, students expand their English vocabulary through a study of Latin root words.

In Latin 2, students review the basic language principles studied in Latin 1 and master new language skills. Emphasis is placed on acquiring the skills needed to read intermediate Latin texts. Further study of Roman colonial expansion, civilization, culture, and religion through an examination of adapted readings in Latin increases the students' awareness of the debt of western civilization to ancient Greece and Rome. Roman settlements of Greece, Egypt, and Britain are heavily featured in geography. Students continue to develop their English vocabulary through a study of Latin roots. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in Latin 1.
courses.prerequisites: Demonstrated proficiency in Latin 1.

courses.description: The in-depth study of Latin in this course provides an opportunity for students to further explore the language, literature, and culture of ancient Rome. The study of classical languages gives important insights into the cultures that produced them, and therefore, leads to a greater understanding of contemporary languages, literature, and cultures. In DP Latin, students complete their study of Latin grammar through authentic reading of Livy’s ab urbe condita and other topical texts. Through this course, students will continue to translate Latin works in context, examining the ideas the ancients expressed, and their artistry within their historical, political and cultural contexts. All students in DP Latin Year 1 have an opportunity to explore a classical area of interest through the completion of the IB internal assessment. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in Latin 2.
courses.prerequisites: Demonstrated proficiency in Latin 2.

courses.description: DP Year 2 is a logical continuation of Year 1. Students spend the majority of this course studying classical literature and culture in depth. Students continue reading and analyzing Livy’s ab urbe condita and other topical texts from year 1. Focus is on artistic and stylistic choices within the texts and tying them to broader themes. Students may decide to culminate the course by completing the May external IB assessment. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in DP Latin - Year 1.

courses.description: This course is designed for students who need more time to build the knowledge and skills presented at the middle school, or have not taken French previously. Students begin their path to proficiency in this introductory French course. Students will use French to communicate on a variety of novice level topics including introducing themselves, talking about their free time activities, school life, making plans with friends, discussing families, their home, and their larger community. Students begin to explore the cultures of France and francophone countries, by examining and analyzing the products, practices and perspectives from these communities. Students will also explore the reasons for learning a second language and strategies for success when learning a new language.

Students continue to develop their communicative proficiency in this French course. Students use French to communicate on a variety of novice level topics including introducing themselves, talking about their fashion choices, describing their routines, making plans with friends, discussing families, their home, and the environment around them (agricultural life). They look at travel, food, shopping, and celebrations in the French speaking world. Students learn to talk about activities in the past tense. Students describe and compare, provide and obtain specific information, express likes and dislikes, and learn to express their needs. Students begin to explore the cultures of France and francophone countries by examining and analyzing the products, practices, and perspectives from these communities. Students also further develop strategies for success when learning a new language. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in French 1.
courses.prerequisites: Demonstrated proficiency in French 1.

courses.description: This is a pivotal year of study for students on the road to language acquisition and communication. This course prepares students for the DP French program. Students continue their path to proficiency in this intermediary French course. Students use French to communicate about a variety of everyday situations such as our use of technology, discussing household responsibilities, reading children’s fairy tales and expressing opinions. These conversational topics can now be expressed in appropriate tenses (present, past, future). Students continue to explore the cultures of francophone countries by examining and analyzing the products, practices, and perspectives from these communities. Short reading selections and authentic literature samples are used to introduce or reinforce vocabulary and grammar structures as well as for their cultural and historical relevance. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in French 2.
courses.prerequisites: Demonstrated proficiency in French 2.

courses.description: In this course, students develop proficiency in the target language through the study of language and culture. In doing so, they develop conceptual understandings of how language works and intercultural understanding. Communication is evidenced through receptive, productive, and interactive skills across a range of contexts and purposes that are appropriate to the level of the course. In this course, students build upon the grammatical foundations of the previous levels while exploring deeper linguistic and cultural themes of global importance. Students explore modern and historical issues such as revolution and war, access to education, art, the environment, and immigration within a global context. Students expand the range of their communication skills by understanding and producing a wide variety of oral and written texts for audiences, contexts, and purposes associated with academic and personal interests. For the development of receptive skills, students must study authentic texts that explore the cultures of the target language. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in French 3.

courses.description: This course is designed for students who need more time to build the knowledge and skills presented at the middle school, have not taken Spanish previously, or moved into the district without previous language experience. In this introductory course, students learn to express themselves in Spanish using basic structures and vocabulary in units organized around everyday themes (i.e. Who I Am and My School, Pastimes and Favorite Activities, Cities and Towns, etc.) with a cultural content. Proficiency at this level is attained by developing the modes of communication (interpersonal, presentational and interpretive) within the thematic contexts. In addition, there is a strong focus on language connections and comparisons in order to interact with cultural competence and to become a lifelong language learner. It is expected that students will attain a novice proficiency level at the end of the course.

This is an entry level course designed to provide students that are interested in career and technical programs an alternative pathway to success in Language Acquisition at MUHS. The course equips students with field-specific language skills that expand their preparedness to enter the workforce. Students can expect to engage in direct whole group instruction on basic conventions of Spanish such as commands, impersonal expression, present tense, and simple past tense. During this time, students will also build foundational skills across all modes of communication (interpersonal, presentational, and interpretive) in order to strengthen conversational and cultural competence in a way that is directly applicable to their integration into the workforce. At the same time, students will follow a personalized curriculum focused on specific vocabulary to help them reach their career goals.

Students continue to expand their arena of conversation to include animals and their habitats, daily routines, childhood, food in the market, and travel. Students talk about their daily routines and learn to talk about past activities. Students describe and compare, provide and obtain specific information, express likes and dislikes, and express needs. Students listen to and read to understand and write or tell a simple story in the past tense. Proficiency at this level is attained by developing the modes of communication (interpersonal, presentational, and interpretive) within the thematic contexts. In addition, there is a strong focus on language connections and comparisons in order to interact with cultural competence and to become a lifelong language learner. It is expected that students will attain a novice mid/high proficiency level at the end of the course. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in Spanish 1.

courses.course_name: Roots of the Modern World, MYP Year 4
courses.description: Roots of the Modern World uses a thematic approach in exploring history, allowing for substantial connections to be made between historical events and the world today. The course explores themes including urbanization, sustainability and world religions. Roots of the Modern World is designed to develop the student in a holistic manner by emphasizing transferable skills that will be of use in other areas of academics and beyond. Throughout the course, students are asked to deeply engage in their own education as inquirers and problem-solvers and reflect upon their process and growth as they do so.
courses.fulfills_text: All 9th and 10th graders must complete the MYP Year 4 and Year 5 courses or equivalent.

courses.description: This course explores the formation and transformation of the United States from its earliest Indigenous civilizations through the end of Reconstruction. Students examine how geography, culture, conflict, and ideology shaped the roots of American democracy and identity. Through inquiry, discussion, and analysis of primary and secondary sources, students investigate key turning points from colonization and revolution to reform and civil war that defined the nation’s early character. The course emphasizes multiple perspectives, the inclusion of historically marginalized voices, and the evolving meaning of freedom and equality. Students will use disciplinary thinking from history, civics, and economics (C3) to evaluate change and continuity over time, build evidence-based arguments, and connect the past to contemporary questions about democracy and justice in the United States.
courses.fulfills_text: All 9th and 10th graders must complete the MYP Year 4 and Year 5 courses or equivalent.

courses.description: This engaging course is designed to deepen students’ understanding of the pivotal events, influential personalities, and transformative ideologies that shaped the 20th century on both a global and national scale. In this class, students explore the interconnectedness of world events and their impact on the United States, examining the social, political, economic, and cultural changes that have defined modern history. Through a thematic and chronological approach, we delve into the major historical milestones and analyze the complex relationships between nations, ideologies, and individuals. Students engage in critical analysis, research, and discussion to develop historical thinking skills. By examining primary and secondary sources, students gain a nuanced understanding of the complexities of historical narratives, encouraging them to think critically about the world around them. Students draw connections between past and present, make informed decisions, and become active, engaged citizens in an ever-changing global landscape.

This course explores the events and realities of the world today through the lens of various approaches to the Social Studies. Students will engage in learning activities that ask them to analyze and understand the world around them. The units include media analysis, the justice system, and other topics that will shift from year to year; skills that students will be developing and the focus on the modern world will be consistent. Students will develop skills in analysis and critical thinking, research, reflection, communication, argumentation, and collaboration, among others.

This course explores world history up to 1500 CE focusing on the question: what happens when cultures come into contact? The course covers cultural interactions through global trade, the impact of disaster on communities, and how the Age of Exploration shaped the roots of the modern world. Students develop skills in historical thinking, comparative analysis, communication, and critical thinking.

Psychology is the study of the human mind and its functions. This course provides an introduction to the basics of that study. Students will learn about topics like nature versus nurture, sleep and dreams, memory, learning and conditioning, psychological ethics and experimentation, and developmental psychology and psychological disorders. Students engage with psychological concepts through reading and reflective writing, research projects, and will even develop and conduct their own psychological experiments.

Because sports play a dominant role both in American society and in the culture of American high schools, it is important for students to understand and appreciate the deeper significance of sports as a major influence on American culture. The purpose of this course is to learn what sports can teach us about issues of race, gender, and violence in American society. Students examine both the historical record and current trends and events that highlight these issues. Students read widely from a variety of scholarly and popular sources, discuss and debate issues with classmates, and conduct significant in-depth research on a case study related to the themes of the course. Students are required to complete several position papers as well as informal and reflective writing about the topics that are covered in class.

This course explores fundamental political concepts such as power, equality, sustainability, and peace in a range of contexts. It allows students to develop an understanding of the local, national, international and global dimensions of political activity and processes, as well as to explore political issues affecting their own lives. The course helps students to understand abstract political concepts by grounding them in real-world examples and case studies. It also invites comparison between such examples and case studies to ensure a wider and transnational perspective. The foundational unit of the course, which comprises the first semester, explores the concepts of power, sovereignty, legitimacy, and interdependence through both theoretical and practical, real world lenses. The Human Rights unit is explored during the second semester. Also in the second semester, students will complete a political engagement activity which requires research, active engagement, and reflection on a political issue. The engagement activity is a DP internal assessment. Recommendation of teacher and successful completion of MYP 4 and 5 required.
This course covers the same topics as Global Politics SL Year 1 but in more depth. Recommendation of teacher and successful completion of MYP 4 and 5 required.

The DP Business Management course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of business theories, concepts, and tools, enabling them to analyze business activities at local, national, and international levels. The curriculum covers key areas such as business organization, human resource management, finance, marketing, and operations management, focusing on their interconnections. Students explore core concepts like change, ethics, globalization, and strategy, developing a holistic view of the business environment. Emphasis is placed on ethical decision-making, strategic thinking, and long-term planning, while students build critical thinking and financial analysis skills. The course encourages exploration of global business issues, equipping students for the international business world. Prerequisite: Successful completion of MYP 4 and 5 required.

courses.course_name: Earth Systems and Physics, MYP Year 4
courses.description: This course explores the origins and connections between physical and geological processes of the Earth system. Students develop their skills in experimental design, data collection and analysis, and scientific communication. The curriculum supports learning through inquiry-based laboratory investigations. The content is aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). The earth science curriculum includes geology, plate tectonics, and astronomy. The physical science curriculum includes gravity, forces, motion, and heat transfer. This course provides the knowledge, skills, and habits of mind needed for problem-solving and ethical decision making in the 21st Century.

Biology is a laboratory course designed to further develop skills learned in Earth Systems and Physics. Particular focus will be given to observation skills, experimental techniques, data collection and analysis, reasoning from experimental data, and reflecting on the impacts of science in modern society. Classroom activities will include many opportunities for hands-on, experiential learning. Topics include biochemical and cellular processes in plants and animals, heredity, evolution, taxonomy, and ecology. This course will connect the local natural world to the classroom, including studies of the Otter Creek and other nearby ecosystems.

Chemistry is an experimental science that combines academic study with the acquisition of practical and investigational skills. This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of chemistry, emphasizing theoretical understanding, practical laboratory skills, and quantitative chemistry. Students explore topics such as atomic structure, bonding, stoichiometry, reactions, and thermochemistry, while also examining the role of chemistry in real-world contexts. The curriculum is designed to develop critical thinking, scientific inquiry, and problem-solving abilities, with an emphasis on inquiry-based learning. Students will be expected to build upon previous skills in experimental design, data collection and analysis, and scientific communication.

This course provides students with in-depth knowledge about a broad-range of topics including biochemistry, cell biology, metabolism, genetics and evolution. This in-depth knowledge is the foundation for essential understanding of broader relationships between structure and function, matter and energy, biological evolution, and the interdependence of organisms. The course focuses on developing students' communication, lab, and critical thinking skills. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP Year 4, and Chemistry.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP Year 4, and Chemistry.

courses.description: This course provides students with in-depth knowledge about a broad range of topics and extends on the content in SL Biology to include biochemistry, cell biology, metabolism, genetics, evolution and ecology. This in-depth knowledge is the foundation for essential understandings of broader relationships between commonality with diversity, form and function, interaction and interdependence and feedback for regulation. The course focuses on developing students’ communication, lab, and critical thinking skills. The DP internal assessment begins at the end of the academic year. Prerequisite: B+ or better in Chemistry.
courses.prerequisites: B+ or better in Chemistry.

courses.description: This course examines a variety of local and global environmental issues facing our present and future generations. Students study ecological principles and engage in field work throughout the year as they investigate Vermont’s soils, wildlife, forests, and aquatic systems. Students look at environmental and sustainability issues through the lens of our food system and how it impacts the environment such as water and air pollution. As students learn about the food system and the associated environmental issues, they learn to grow their own food as well as grow food for the MUHS school cafeteria using the MUHS greenhouse. Research projects include a river study of the Otter Creek, Vermont Fish and Wildlife fur bearing project, and community based projects throughout the Middlebury area. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP4, and Biology - MYP5, Chemistry, or equivalent.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP4, and Biology - MYP5, Chemistry, or equivalent.

courses.course_name: Technical Design and Build  1 Credit Science or Design
courses.description: Using the design and engineering loop as the theme of the course, students are faced with hands-on, real world problems with a focus on designing and building projects. Science, technology, engineering, and math concepts (STEM) are embedded in all of the units. Concepts such as reverse engineering, Newton’s laws of motion, and simply machines are covered. Students pick an engineering design project that focuses on solving a problem in the community as their final summative assessment for this course. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP Year 4, and Biology - MYP5, Chemistry, or equivalent.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP Year 4, and Biology - MYP5, Chemistry, or equivalent.
courses.notes: Also listed under Design (350: Technical Design and Build, Grades 11-12, 1 Credit - Science or Design, page 35)

courses.course_name: DP Environmental Systems and Societies (SL), Year 1
courses.description: Environmental Systems and Societies (ESS) is an interdisciplinary course designed to combine the methodology, techniques, and knowledge associated with the Sciences and those associated with Individuals and Societies. Topics for the first year of the course include ecosystems, biodiversity, water use, and aquatic food production. Because it is an interdisciplinary course, it can count as either a science credit or an Individuals and Societies credit (or as both, by splitting the credits between the two years). Prerequisite: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP Year 4, and Biology - MYP5, Chemistry or equivalent.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP Year 4, and Biology - MYP5, Chemistry or equivalent.
courses.fulfills_text: it can count as either a science credit or an Individuals and Societies credit (or as both, by splitting the credits between the two years)
courses.notes: Also listed under Sciences section as a cross-reference; Individuals and Societies entry (p.24) points to this full description. Counts as science or Individuals and Societies credit.

courses.description: Physics is the most fundamental of the experimental sciences, as it seeks to understand the relationship between objects and their energies. During this first year of the two-year course of study, DP HL Physics topics include measurements and uncertainties, mechanics, thermal physics, waves, and electromagnetism. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Chemistry, or Math teacher recommendation. .
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Chemistry, or Math teacher recommendation. .

courses.description: This course is an extension of Year 1 DP Biology (HL). Topics covered include biodiversity and physiology. The DP internal assessment is finished in the beginning of the academic year. Students are given numerous class meetings to work on their independent investigations. Prerequisite: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.
courses.prerequisites: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.

courses.course_name: DP Environmental Systems and Societies (SL), Year 2
courses.description: In the second year of this course, students explore more of the human impacts on our environment. Topics for the second year of this course include soil systems, atmospheric systems, climate change, energy production, and human resource use, along with an overview/review of the course prior to the external exam. It is the expectation that all students taking ESS Year 2 complete an Internal Assessment. Prerequisite: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.
courses.prerequisites: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.
courses.notes: Also listed under Sciences section as a cross-reference; Individuals and Societies entry (p.24) points to this full description. Counts as science or Individuals and Societies credit.

courses.description: This course is a continuation of Chemistry. Topics covered include thermochemistry, chemical kinetics, equilibrium, acids and bases, redox processes, and organic chemistry. The DP internal assessment occurs late in the academic year. Students are given numerous class meetings to work on their independent investigations. Prerequisite: Students must complete Chemistry before beginning DP Chemistry Year 2.
courses.prerequisites: Students must complete Chemistry before beginning DP Chemistry Year 2.

courses.description: This is the second year of the DP (HL) Physics course of study. Topics include fields, circular motion and gravitation, quantum physics, nuclear and particle physics, and energy production. . A focus of the second year is preparing for, and completing, the internal assessment which is submitted to IB. Prerequisite: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.
courses.prerequisites: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.

courses.description: This course is part of the Middle Years International Baccalaureate Program designed to prepare students for Algebra 1 and the Standard Level Diploma math courses. The topics for this course are aligned with the Common Core Standards for mathematics and include the following: factoring, computation with rational numbers, writing and solving linear expressions and equations, inequalities, direct variations, and properties of rational numbers including exponents.

This course is part of the Middle Years International Baccalaureate Program designed to prepare students for Standard Level Diploma Program math courses. The topics for this course are aligned with the Common Core Standards for high school mathematics and include the following: linear, exponential, and absolute value functions, direct and inverse variation, linear equations and inequalities, systems of linear equations and inequalities, rules of exponents, and quadratic equations.

This course is part of the Middle Years International Baccalaureate Program, designed to prepare students for the Standard Level Diploma Program math courses. Mathematical concepts are developed through inquiry. The topics for this course are aligned with the Common Core Standards for high school mathematics and include the following: deductive reasoning, coordinate geometry, properties of triangles, quadrilaterals & polygons, congruence and similarly, right triangle trigonometry, circles, surface area and volume, one & two variable statistics, Venn diagrams, set notation, and probability. Prerequisite: Algebra 1 (MA110)
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1 (MA110)

courses.description: This course is designed to prepare students for the Standard Level or Higher Level Diploma Program math courses, and/or for college or university studies. Mathematical concepts are developed through inquiry. The topics for this course are aligned with the Common Core State Standards for high school mathematics and include the following: functions, quadratics and quadratic equations, exponents and exponential equations, logarithms and logarithmic functions, inequalities, and topics in geometry including similarity, trigonometry, circles and volume and surface area. Prerequisite: Recommendation of Algebra 1 teacher or 8th grade math teacher and demonstration of proficiency of Algebra 1 on diagnostic exam(s).
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of Algebra 1 teacher or 8th grade math teacher and demonstration of proficiency of Algebra 1 on diagnostic exam(s).

courses.description: This course engages students with real-world financial applications while maintaining deep mathematical rigor. Each of the course’s 10 units blends one core personal finance topic with one relevant math concept. Financial topics include taxes, checking, savings, budgeting, investing, managing credit, and insurance. Relevant math topics include: linear equations, systems of linear equations, inequalities, exponential equations, modeling functions, statistical analysis, probability and an introduction to calculating with spreadsheets. Prerequisite: Algebra 2 with Geometry (MA225) or Geometry, Probability and Statistics (MA215).
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 2 with Geometry (MA225) or Geometry, Probability and Statistics (MA215).

courses.description: This course is the first in a two-year sequence. It is designed for students who enjoy describing the real world and solving practical problems using mathematics. In addition, it is for those students who are interested in using graphing calculators to explore mathematical models and enjoy the more practical side of mathematics. Topics include number and algebra, functions (quadratic, cubic, exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric), sequences and series, geometry of solids, trigonometry applications, coordinate geometry, linear regression, and probability. Prerequisite: Algebra 2 with Geometry (MA225), Financial Algebra (MA306), or recommendation of Geometry, Probability and Statistics (MA215) teacher.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 2 with Geometry (MA225), Financial Algebra (MA306), or recommendation of Geometry, Probability and Statistics (MA215) teacher.

courses.description: This course is the first in a two-year sequence. It is intended for students who wish to pursue studies in mathematics at university or subjects that have a large mathematical content; it is for students who enjoy developing mathematical arguments, problem-solving and exploring real and abstract applications, with and without technology. Strong algebra skills are required. Topics in the first year include functions (linear, quadratic, rational, exponential, and logarithmic), sequences and series, geometry, trigonometry, linear regression, and probability. Prerequisite: Recommendation of Algebra 2 with Geometry (MA225) teacher.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of Algebra 2 with Geometry (MA225) teacher.

courses.description: This course is the first in a two year sequence. It is intended for students who wish to pursue studies in mathematics in post-secondary studies, or subjects that have a large mathematical content; it is for students who enjoy developing mathematical arguments, problem-solving and exploring real and abstract applications, with and without technology. Students who take this course should have very strong algebra skills, be highly motivated and passionate about mathematics. Topics included in the first year include: functions (polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric), proof, trigonometric identities, differential calculus, and probability. Prerequisite: Recommendation of Analysis and Approaches SL1 (Math 320) teacher.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of Analysis and Approaches SL1 (Math 320) teacher.

courses.description: This course is the second in a two-year sequence. It is designed for students who enjoy describing the real world and solving practical problems using mathematics. In addition, it is for those students who are interested in using technology to explore mathematical models and enjoy the more practical side of mathematics. Other topics include statistics (errors, methods, descriptive, and hypothesis testing), probability distributions, financial applications of geometric series, and an introduction to both differential and integral calculus and their applications. In addition, students complete a mathematical exploration on a topic of their choosing. Prerequisites: Applications and Interpretations SL1 (MA310) or Analysis and Approaches SL1 (MA320).
courses.prerequisites: Applications and Interpretations SL1 (MA310) or Analysis and Approaches SL1 (MA320).

courses.description: This course is the second in a two-year sequence. It is intended for students who wish to pursue studies in mathematics at university or subjects that have a large mathematical content. Topics in the second year include statistics, differential and integral calculus, and probability distributions. In addition, students complete a mathematical exploration on a topic of their choosing. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Analysis and Approaches SL1 (MA320).
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Analysis and Approaches SL1 (MA320).

courses.description: This course is the second in a two year sequence. It is intended for students who wish to pursue studies in mathematics in post-secondary studies, or subjects that have a large mathematical content. Students who take this course should have very strong algebra skills, be highly motivated and passionate about mathematics. Topics include: statistics, complex numbers, vectors, differential calculus, integral calculus, and probability distributions. In addition, students will complete a mathematical exploration on a topic of their choosing. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Analysis and Approaches HL1 (MA321).
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Analysis and Approaches HL1 (MA321).

courses.course_name: Beat Making and Music Production MYP
courses.description: This contemporary course is open to any student with an interest in music. This is a project-based course in which students have opportunities to learn basic musical concepts. The course covers contemporary music theory, songwriting techniques, and the use of music technology for audio recording and production.

The prerequisite for this course is a minimum of two years of ensemble experience or with the permission of the director. Requirements include: two to three yearly concerts, small ensemble performances, parades, as well as individual and group projects based on units studied or music performed.

Enrollment in this course will be by audition in the spring. This select group will ideally consist of five saxophones, five trumpets, four trombones and five rhythm instruments. Students are required to be enrolled in Band (with the exception of the guitar and bass). Students are expected to improvise and learn concepts of improvisation such as major/minor scales and modes. Students may be asked to learn jazz standards and stylize them, arrange jazz charts and compose jazz melodies. Students are expected to attend adjudications and competitions as well as public performances throughout the school year.

This course is open to any students with beginning proficiency on drums, guitar, bass, or piano/keyboard. This is a project-based course in which students will study and perform contemporary music styles including (but not limited to) rock, pop, reggae, hip-hop, and folk/country. The class focuses on performance but will also include contemporary music theory, basic music literacy, and songwriting techniques.

Concert Choir is MUHS’s vocal performing group of students in grades 9-12. Students improve their knowledge of singing as well as improving their music reading skills. Concert Choir students are required to attend all public performances (usually three to four per year).

Choral Ensemble is an auditioned ensemble of accelerated singers working to develop their individual artistic skills and overall musicianship. Enrollment in this course will be by audition in the spring for grades 8-11.

Students learn basic techniques of the piano. They learn basic music theory, music literacy and how to play chords and melodic lines on the piano. No prior piano or music experience is needed. Pianos (keyboards) will be supplied by the school.

Students will learn how to read music using the guitar. They will learn basic music theory and how to play chords and melodic lines on the guitar. No prior guitar or music experience is needed. Guitars will be supplied by the school.

Students will explore concepts of music theory in detail through analysis, arranging, ear training and composition. At the conclusion of the course, students will have a strong understanding of the structure of musical compositions and be fully prepared for the more in depth study of music and music performance requirements in the DP Music course.

The DP music course provides students with the opportunity to engage in the world of music as lifelong participants. Students study musical analysis, composition, and performance. By the end of this course, students demonstrate knowledge of music in relation to time, place, and cultures as well as use appropriate musical terminology to describe and reflect their critical understanding of music. Students act as researchers, performers, and creators. All students develop critical-thinking skills through reflection and analysis of their craft. It is required that all students participating in DP music are enrolled in the school’s music performance ensemble. Due to the diploma program performance portfolio, students need to audition or provide evidence of competency on one instrument.

The DP music course provides students with the opportunity to engage in the world of music as lifelong participants. Students study musical analysis, composition, and performance. By the end of this two-year course, students demonstrate knowledge, understanding, and perception of music in relation to time, place, and cultures as well as appropriate musical terminology to describe and reflect their critical understanding of music. Students act as researchers, performers, and creators. All students develop critical-thinking skills through reflective thought and analysis of their craft. It is required that all students participating in DP music are enrolled in the school’s music performance ensemble. Due to the diploma program performance portfolio, students need to audition or provide evidence of competency on one instrument.

DP Music Year 2 is an intensive course for students who have completed DP Music Year 1 and are working towards either the IB certificate or the IB Diploma. In Year 2, students work towards completion of the IB internal assessment requirements: Exploring Music (2400 word essay, music composition, musical song adaptation, and musical composition and performance), Experimenting with Music (1500 word essay, three musical experiments as a performer, three musical experiments as a creator), and Performing Music, (600 word essay, 12 minutes of performance, 6 minutes of creating exercise). Prerequisite: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.
courses.prerequisites: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.

courses.description: DP Music Year 2 is an intensive course for students who have completed DP Music Year 1 and are working towards either the IB certificate or the IB Diploma. In Year 2, students work towards completion of the IB assessment requirements. At the end of Year 2, students are required to submit the following portfolios: Exploring Music (2400 word essay, musical composition, musical song adaptation, and musical performance), Experimenting with Music (1500 word essay, three musical experiments as a performer, three musical experiments as a creator), and Performing Music, (600 word essay, 12 minutes of performance, 6 minutes of creating exercise), and The Contemporary Music Maker (HL only. This is a 15 minute multimedia collaborative project). Prerequisite: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.
courses.prerequisites: Students must complete Year 1 of this course before beginning Year 2.

courses.course_name: The Creative Process in Studio Art, MYP
courses.description: In this Visual Arts course, students engage in a variety of materials and methods in order to build and strengthen art-making skills, including: collage, drawing, pen & ink, printmaking, zine-making, watercolor, acrylics, digital tools, ceramics, jewelry, graphic design, sculpture, and more. Students practice the fundamental concepts used to create effective artwork and then work to create final pieces that demonstrate their learning. Students participate in research and inquiry to understand the factors that influence the creation of artwork, and practice creative thinking skills to develop and use their creative voice. Students also receive and populate a multimedia sketchbook, chronicling their creative journey.

This is an advanced studio course designed to offer students the opportunity to develop ideas and technical skills at a higher level. Investigating established artists' works and understanding the context and meaning behind these artworks will contribute to students' own artmaking and idea development. The course will begin with guided practice in art-making skills. As the semester progresses, students will gain independence as they develop their own ideas, practice skills, and complete resolved independent artworks. Students participate in the annual art exhibition, developing and carrying out an independent exhibition of their own artworks. Prerequisite: Students must have completed 1 credit of visual art coursework prior to enrolling in this class.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have completed 1 credit of visual art coursework prior to enrolling in this class.

courses.description: Through demonstration, practice, and observation, students in this course work to strengthen their drawing skills. Students learn and apply the fundamentals of composition, art, and design to their drawings. Students work with a variety of drawing mediums and practice new techniques as part of coursework. Students use a variety of drawing materials, including graphite, drawing, and pen and ink, as they work to refine their technique.

The course is designed to introduce students to the fundamentals of painting using a variety of painting media. Students learn to control their values, edges, color, and composition. This course explores a variety of subject matter and painting techniques. Prerequisite: Students must have completed either Drawing or Creative Process in Studio Art prior to enrolling in this course.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have completed either Drawing or Creative Process in Studio Art prior to enrolling in this course.

courses.description: This course covers the fundamentals of art and three-dimensional design. Students apply these concepts in creating three-dimensional artworks. Students have the opportunity to work with a variety of materials and methods used in creating sculpture, including clay. Students investigate the definition of sculpture, its origin and history, and its evolution over time to understand the factors that influence the creation of artwork.

This course introduces students to digital imaging techniques. The course is taught from a fine art perspective with a continual focus on artistic composition and photographic communication. Students gain a deeper understanding of the elements of art and principles of design as they relate to artistic decision-making and photographic aesthetics. The work of great photographers and movements is integrated to support these aims. This is a hands-on art course that requires students to engage with digital technology and computer literacy. A digital camera is provided for in-class use.

In this course, students explore the use of materials to create well-designed objects that adorn the body. They learn techniques of metalworking including, forging, cold connections, and soldering. Through the study of ancient and modern techniques, students also explore the history of this craft and its contexts in culture.

This course is designed for students who have a solid foundation in the basics of jewelry making and are eager to explore more complex and challenging designs. Students delve deeply into the creative design process to produce sophisticated and personalized jewelry pieces. Students cultivate a personal design aesthetic and effectively communicate their designs through sketching, rendering, and prototyping. Prerequisite: Students must complete Jewelry and Metalwork before enrolling in this course.
courses.prerequisites: Students must complete Jewelry and Metalwork before enrolling in this course.

courses.description: This course may be taken as a one-year advanced art course or combined with Year 2 of the course for students interested in the IB Diploma Program or certificate. The course encourages students to challenge their own creative and cultural expectations as artists. It is an intensive and thought-provoking course in which dedicated students apply the creative process to develop technical proficiency and confidence as art-makers. In addition to creating art, students learn how to formally analyze artworks from a variety of contexts while reflecting on how these artworks impact their own art-making practices. At the end of Year 1, students will have completed the research and writing of the comparative study (an IB-required assessment task), in which they compare artworks from different cultures through a written report. Additionally, students will have developed a portfolio that demonstrates growth and proficiency in a wide range of artistic concepts, skills, and techniques. Prerequisite: Portfolio review or successful completion of 1 fine art credit required.
courses.prerequisites: Portfolio review or successful completion of 1 fine art credit required.

courses.description: This course expands upon DP Visual Art SL with additional assessment requirements at HL that allow for breadth and greater depth in the teaching and learning. The assessment tasks require HL students to reflect on how their own work has been influenced by exposure to other artists and for them to experiment in greater depth with additional art-making media, techniques, and forms. HL students are encouraged to produce a larger body of resolved works and to demonstrate a deeper consideration of how their resolved works communicate with a potential viewer. This rigorous course encourages highly dedicated art students to challenge their own creative and cultural expectations and boundaries. Prerequisite: Portfolio review and successful completion of 1 fine art credit required.
courses.prerequisites: Portfolio review and successful completion of 1 fine art credit required.

courses.description: This course is an intensive course for students who have completed DP Visual Art Year 1 or portfolio review and are working towards either an IB certificate or the IB Diploma. In Year 2, students are working towards completion of the IB DP requirements: the comparative study, process portfolio, and exhibition. This course requires students to be self-directed and demonstrate an ability to manage long-term and complex assignments, while working towards technical proficiency and confidence as art-makers and thinkers. The course culminates with an independent exhibition of the student’s own work and submission of all IB assessment criteria. Prerequisite: Successful completion of DP Visual Art Year 1 required.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of DP Visual Art Year 1 required.

courses.description: This course expands upon DP Visual Art SL with additional assessment requirements at HL that allow for breadth and greater depth in the teaching and learning. The assessment tasks require HL students to reflect on how their own work has been influenced by exposure to other artists and for them to experiment in greater depth with additional art making media, techniques and forms. HL students are encouraged to produce a larger body of resolved works and to demonstrate a deeper consideration of how their resolved works communicate with a potential viewer. This rigorous course encourages highly dedicated art students to challenge their own creative and cultural expectations and boundaries. Prerequisite: Successful completion of DP Visual Art Year 1 required.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of DP Visual Art Year 1 required.

courses.description: Artisan Studio invites students to explore craftsmanship as a form of creative expression in a world increasingly dominated by mass production. Through woodworking, leatherworking, 3D printing, and laser fabrication, students learn to design and create original handmade works that emphasize quality, artistry, and attention to detail. Projects focus on aesthetic decision-making, creative problem-solving, and material exploration. Students leave the course with a strong foundation in craftsmanship and an understanding of how these skills connect to real-world applications where handmade, well-crafted products are highly valued.

Artisan Studio 2 builds upon the creative and technical foundations established in Artisan Studio 1, challenging students to apply their knowledge to larger, more complex artistic problems. Students engage in advanced projects and design challenges that integrate woodworking, leather, laser fabrication, and 3D design. The course emphasizes independent inquiry, refined craftsmanship, and artistic innovation. Students also explore how their skills and creations can connect to real-world opportunities—developing an appreciation for the growing market that values handmade, high-quality, and sustainably crafted goods. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Artisan Studio 1.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Artisan Studio 1.

courses.description: In this hands-on, project-based course, students will learn the fundamentals of computer programming while exploring the tools and technologies used to create computer and video games. Through engaging activities, students will gain experience in block coding, text-based programming, and the dynamic field of artificial intelligence (AI). Additionally, the course provides opportunities to work with robotics and drones, offering practical insights into their real-world applications. The robotics and drone components focus primarily on coding, creativity, and design—not mechanical engineering—helping students understand how software brings digital and physical designs to life. No prior programming experience is necessary, making this course accessible to beginners.

All students in grade 9 take this course. This class explores a variety of lifetime activities, introducing fitness skills and concepts and aesthetic movement through dance. The physical education curriculum uses national and state standards to guide instruction in order to provide students with opportunities to develop knowledge and skills in a variety of activities which will improve fitness levels and foster personal growth and confidence. Each standards based unit is designed to teach the students the concepts and skills necessary for them to participate successfully and safely.

All students in grade 9 take this course. This course will explore how to incorporate health components and skills into the increasingly independent lives of adolescents. Standards based instruction is used to provide students with opportunities to develop knowledge and skills in a variety of topics, which will foster personal growth and confidence. Each unit is designed to teach the concepts and skills necessary for students to take care of different components of their wellness. These units include motivation for individual wellness, substance education, interpersonal relationships, sexual wellness, mental wellness, and the taking care of the physical body. This course plays an integral role in the well-rounded growth and learning of all students and will help them to develop the foundation for a healthy lifestyle.

All students in grade 10 take this course. This class combines physical activity with learning about healthy lifestyle practices. Students further their knowledge and understanding of how to develop personal wellness through fitness, nutrition, sleep, hydration, and mindfulness habits in order to positively impact how they feel and perform. Students explore lifetime activities in order to promote wellness and complete an aesthetic movement unit which will include yoga, Tai Chi, pilates, and step aerobics.

All students in grade 10 take this course. Students will learn and apply healthy lifestyle practices through a variety of engaging activities–such as self reflection, guest speakers, group collaboration, and independent project assessments. This course aims to provide structured and natural exploration of all areas of wellness. This course will cover the following topics: mental wellness, substance education, diversity/sense of belonging, healthy relationships/communication, sexual wellness, diseases, and first aid. This course plays an integral role in students’ abilities to understand and access community resources, make informed and practical decisions, and develop a sense of autonomy surrounding their own health and wellness.

This course builds on content and knowledge learned in MYP4 and MYP5 PE to improve students' fitness levels through a variety of fitness activities. Students experience different ways to develop fitness as well as participate in a self-designed fitness routine based on their personal goals. This course facilitates a greater understanding of how to condition appropriately, and demonstrates that there are many ways to develop a physically active lifestyle. Students are challenged to develop good habits of exercise, nutrition, hydration, and rest, as well as make connections between regular physical activity and their social, emotional, and cognitive wellness. The independent and individualized nature of this course helps students develop the foundation for a lifetime of physical activity and wellness.

The primary purpose of this course is to teach students the skills and understanding required for successful, high-level academic research and writing. Topics explored include choosing relevant sources, citing sources appropriately, academic honesty, determining appropriate methodology across different subject areas, and writing using academic language. Additionally, full DP candidates will learn about extended essay requirements and receive guidance on choosing a subject and topic, as well as crafting a feasible research question. This course is required for DP candidates.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is required for DP candidates.

courses.description: Theory of Knowledge is a course focused on the question, “How do we know what we know?” In TOK, students explore how we produce, acquire, share, revise, and verify knowledge in real-world contexts. The curriculum comprises the exploration of themes such as knowledge and the knower, eight ways of knowing, and areas of knowledge. Students can take this semester-long version of TOK in either grade 11 or 12. TOK Part 1 or Midd Core TOK Part 1 is required for graduation.
courses.fulfills_text: TOK Part 1 or Midd Core TOK Part 1 is required for graduation.

courses.description: In this elective course, an extension of the required TOK Part 1, students continue to focus on the question, “How do we know what we know” by diving deeper into knowledge questions via five areas of knowledge and the respective organizational framework of four elements: scope, perspectives, methods and tools, and ethics. This course allows for and requires students to explore individual knowledge topics. Prerequisite: Successful completion of 300: MC TOK Part 1.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of 300: MC TOK Part 1.

courses.description: In addition to covering the same topics as the Midd Core TOK, this class centers on exploring knowledge questions that are organized into a framework of four elements: scope, perspectives, methods and tools, and ethics. In Part I, students focus on the core and optional themes in preparation for the IB internal assessment, the TOK Exhibition. Following the Research and Writing Readiness for the Extended Essay course in semester 1, DP candidates begin TOK Part 1 during the semester 2 of grade 11. This course runs over two years. The second half takes place during semester 1 of grade 12. Successful completion of this course is required for all DP candidates.
courses.fulfills_text: Successful completion of this course is required for all DP candidates.

courses.description: This course is an extension of the first semester, from the previous year. Students focus on examining Areas of Knowledge in preparation for the culminating IB external assessment, the TOK Essay. This course is only offered first semester of the grade 12 year in order to allow full diploma candidates to meet the timeline for submitting their two required IB diploma assessments.

In this course, students explore all aspects of dealing with their own finances. This includes learning about budgeting, checking accounts, savings accounts, credit cards, loans, insurance, apartment renting, car buying, investing, financial aid for post-secondary education, and other important financial skills. The class challenges students to look at their own personal spending habits now and in the future. This is a class for everyone who wants to be a better informed consumer and be able to make educated decisions about what to do with their money.

What happens after high school? What are the options available to students once high school is finished? This course helps students determine career interests and research the different paths that can lead to different careers. Whether headed to college, vocational school, an apprenticeship, or into the job market after high school, it is important to be on the right path. Students do interest inventories, research different career clusters and post-secondary institutions, hear a variety of speakers from different areas, and find out what it takes to get hired in today’s competitive job market.

This course is designed for students who want to explore the tools for successful small business ownership. In this class, students develop a business plan for the business of their choice. Students choose a product or service that interests them and develop their business plan from there. This is a great course for anyone who is involved in a family business or would like to start a business in the future.

Learn the four P’s of Marketing: price, product, place, and promotion. Students develop a marketing plan for a product that they determine on their own. Students then conduct a market research project on the products to see if and how they will sell in the marketplace. Students decide where their products will be sold, for how much, and how to market their products. The course culminates with a segment on how business and marketing firms target young people so that everyone becomes a better-educated consumer. This is a great introduction to the world of marketing and business.

Where does Middlebury fit into the world economy? How does the world economy affect us here in Vermont? These questions and many more are answered in this course on how the world of international business works. Students learn how the economies of the world work together, why they work together, and what happens when they do not work together. Each student focuses on one country and how that country’s economy is affected by the globalization of business that affects us all.

Students attend their internship when they are not scheduled for a class or after school. Requirements include attending the internship on a weekly basis, turning in timesheets that explain what the student does on a daily basis at the internship, and meeting regularly with the Work-based Learning Coordinator. Academic credit is given based on the number of hours engaged in the internship. This opportunity is open to all students.

This class stresses basic food preparation techniques and basic nutrition. Students use their knowledge to plan and prepare nutritious meals that they enjoy serving and eating. Students also have the opportunity to explore new foods.

Students use the same skills and knowledge gained in beginning foods. In addition, students travel around the world using their taste buds, exploring the foods of Asia, Greece, France, Mexico, Germany, etc. This is a fun class full of wonderful tastes and aromas. The students prepare all the meals themselves. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Beginning Foods.

This program teaches students workplace skills that will help any person succeed and grow in any area of work and/or career exploration that the student chooses. The work-site supervisor and the Work-based Learning Coordinator work with students to teach these essential skills. Requirements include working at the job-site and agreed upon set of hours, meeting regularly with the Work-based Learning Coordinator, and turning in paycheck stubs. Credit is determined by the amount of hours put in at the work-site each academic quarter. This opportunity is open to students age 14 and older.

In doing this work, students participate in the life of the community, learn about career possibilities, gain knowledge and skills needed for responsible membership in their communities, and understand more about social issues. To receive credit, students attend one group meeting to share their experiences with others, keep a journal, and complete a final project about the organization they served. All grades are Pass/Fail. The hours completed in community service can apply toward the CAS requirement of the IB Diploma Program.

Lifetime and recreational activities include archery, golf, soccer, basketball, badminton, softball, Bocce, and gymnastics. A fitness program is implemented based on the individual’s FitnessGram Assessment in the beginning of the course. Health topics in this course include male and female anatomy, adolescence, puberty changes, conception, stages of pregnancy, contraceptive methods, and sexually transmitted diseases. courses.description: Food Systems Science is a course designed to educate and empower students to make informed decisions about their bodies. Students will learn about the three pillars of Human Sustainability - Mind, Body and Fuel. They will learn about the interconnected parts and their relationship to the industrial food system and more sustainable alternatives. It will include information on food's impact on human health, biodiversity and the environment. Students will examine the food system’s affects on consumers and their communities. The course will culminate with a “Food System Action Project”, where each student will identify a food system problem and design an intervention to address it. A large component of the course will include active learning in context through growing greens in the MUHS greenhouse and managing the student-run Hidden Brain Cafe. Prerequisites: MYP4 or EPIC, with teacher recommendation and IEP Team approval.

Those decisions are made on an individual basis, as some students and sites require constant supervision or support. Students are evaluated by the work-site supervisors and their job coach. Classroom work includes maintaining an updated resume, practice searching for jobs, and filling out applications. Students who complete an additional portfolio may receive 0.5 Language/Literature credit. We have amazing community partners around Middlebury! Possible internship sites include retail, restaurant, technology, agriculture, automotive, and manufacturing.

At the end of quarter 3, families are invited out to the boat-shop where each student demonstrates one aspect of the building process. On launch day, students give a brief presentation on their experience before embarking on the first row in the new boat.

courses.description: The ability to understand, speak, pronounce, read, and write basic English is critical to the social and academic participation of any American high school student. Beginning ELD introduces students whose primary language is not English to the basics of the language. Students practice listening, speaking, reading, writing, and viewing English through drills, dialogues, skits, discussion, tasks, guided reading, dictation that emphasize comprehensible input and communicative competence. ML students practice conversing in a variety of situations and develop basic reading and writing skills and strategies. They also gain a working knowledge of school and community culture and how to use technology to produce classroom work. Language and Literature credit may be awarded with administrative approval.

More information is available in the School Counseling Office.

The partnering colleges are the Community College of Vermont, Vermont State University, and Vermont Technical College/Vermont Academy of Science and Technology. Students interested in this program should see their school counselor. Students apply for admission during their junior year.

courses.description: Middlebury Union High School has an agreement with Middlebury College whereby a limited number of grade 12 students are allowed to enroll in Middlebury College courses that the high school does not offer. To apply, students must have exhausted all MUHS classes offered in the subject area to which they are applying. There is no charge for these courses. All applicants must be exceptionally strong academic students who have demonstrated a responsible and mature approach to their academic commitments. Interested students need to complete an application form (available in the School Counseling Office). Classes are taken for an academic letter grade and become part of the official transcript. They count towards Class Decile Rank and Grade Point Average (GPA). No college credit is awarded for courses taken at Middlebury College by a MUHS student.

Branching Out is a flexible, project-based course where students design their own learning around their interests and goals while earning credit in any discipline. The course culminates in a presentation to a panel, where students showcase their learning and the impact of their work.

Independent study courses are designed for students who are unable to reasonably participate in regularly scheduled classes or who desire academic pursuits outside the available curriculum. Approval for an independent study depends on the student’s level of maturity, responsibility, self-motivation and academic performance. To apply, students select a topic and complete an application with their school counselor.

The Raven Ridge Program at MUHS provides a smaller, more supportive environment for students to engage in their core academic classes. The Raven Ridge team includes a lead teacher and paraeducator, as well as other teachers who work with students to attain content area credit and aid students as they work toward graduation. Students who are part of the Raven Ridge program have individualized and flexible schedules to meet their personalized needs and goals. Students interested in enrolling in the program must complete an application and meet with their school counselor to discuss their interests and goals.

Students interested in earning credit for course work outside Middlebury Union High School’s offerings must complete the “Request for Pre-Approval” form available in the School Counseling Office prior to the beginning of the course. Additional information such as a course syllabus and course description should be included with the request. Credit for coursework taken outside MUHS will be for elective credit unless otherwise approved. If approved, the student must submit an official grade report to the School Counseling office upon completion of the course to receive credit. Examples of potential alternative course work are Johns Hopkins Center for Talented Youth (CTY), Middlebury World Language Programs, or Keystone Online.

The Learning Lab is a hub of academic learning at the heart of the MUHS school building. Students can enroll in Learning Lab to access a wide range of learning opportunities and services. The basic structure is a supported study hall. Students enrolled in Learning Lab may engage in credit-bearing independent studies through the Branching Out program. Content area teachers are assigned to the Learning Lab at various parts of the day to provide support and/or tutoring. Additional supports and services may be available as needed. The Learning Lab is open each day from 8:00 AM to 3:30 PM. Students can be enrolled for a block at a time, or they can drop in as needed for additional support.
